When a change needs an engineer

Experiment settings were closely tied to pipeline implementation. Changing audience allocation or a cashback rule could require an analyst to request a code change. New scenarios added conditions and branches, while the interaction between rules became harder to explain. The challenge was to let analysts make some changes independently without losing control over their meaning: which parameters are valid, how they combine, and what happens when something is wrong.

Turning intent into configuration

I worked on a declarative model that brings the experiment description together: its audience, participation conditions and actions affecting cashback. I discussed launch scenarios and limitations with analysts, using those conversations to develop both the model and its documentation. Configuration has to make sense to the person defining the experiment. They need to understand the outcome of combining parameters, supported by examples, useful error messages and predictable execution.

Several rules, one customer

A separate challenge was supporting independent experiments that can affect the same customer. A single participation flag is not enough: membership and the order of applying changes need distinct representations. I contributed to this logic and to extending a shared approach across product areas. Configuration and runtime checks help contain that complexity. The shared model was used across three areas, while genuinely new types of behaviour still require engineering work.

Making the result explainable

I worked on information about applied experiments and intermediate processing results. It helps reconstruct which rules affected a final cashback assignment. Related platform work included Kafka-based delivery, data contracts, PostgreSQL-backed shipping cursors and lag metrics. Getting a result is only part of the job. A useful system also makes processing state understandable: where work stopped, which changes have already been applied, and what information is available to investigate a question.

What changed

Some experiments and rule changes can be prepared as configuration without modifying application logic. Analysts gain independence within defined boundaries; engineers remain responsible for the meaning and validation of those boundaries. This is not a universal builder: a new action requires changes to the model, tests and documentation. The case explains that mechanism without claiming a measured speedup or business impact. The visual example on this page uses fictional data and independently authored rules.

Good configuration gives people control over the changes they need to make—and makes the consequences understandable.
